extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, litigators, and judges evaluating 35 U.S.C. §101 patent-eligibility
extracted.subtask_description: Applying the two-step Alice/Mayo framework to determine whether claimed patent subject matter is directed to an abstract idea, natural phenomenon, or law of nature and, if so, whether the claim includes an 'inventive concept' sufficient to transform the claim into a patent-eligible application. Focuses on claim language, specification, and whether claimed components are conventional or perform only basic functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the two-step Mayo/Alice framework
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the two-step Mayo/Alice framework: (1) determine whether the claim is directed to an unpatentable law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea; (2) if so, determine whether the claim includes an 'inventive concept' sufficient to transform the nature of the claim into a patent-eligible application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Alice Corp. v. CLS Bank and Mayo Collaborative Servs.; perform both steps sequentially and explicitly. Step 1 asks what the claim is 'directed to'; step 2 asks whether an inventive concept exists that transforms the abstract idea into a patent-eligible application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify the 'focus of the claimed advance' at step one
rubrics_metrics.description: At step one, ask 'what the patent asserts to be the focus of the claimed advance over the prior art,' focusing on the language of the asserted claims considered in light of the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow TecSec, Inc. v. Adobe Inc.; base the directed-to inquiry on claim language and specification rather than generalized characterizations. The claimed focus (not merely the field) controls the analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims directed to results/effects that are abstract ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is directed to an abstract idea if it claims a result or effect that itself is the abstract idea and merely invokes generic processes and machinery rather than a specific means or method that improves the relevant technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Smart Sys. Innovations and Elec. Power Grp. reasoning: if the claimed advance is a goal/result implemented by generic components, treat it as an abstract idea. Example: 'producing a resultant digital image ... enhanced with said second digital image' characterized as an abstract idea of enhancing one picture with another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conventional components performing basic functions do not supply inventiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Recitation of well-known, routine, conventional components (e.g., image sensors, lenses, analog-to-digital converters, memory, generic processors) that perform only their basic functions at a high level of generality does not render a claim patent-eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim lists commonplace components and they 'perform only their basic functions' or are recited at a high level of generality, that supports ineligibility (see In re TLI Commc’ns and Alice step two analysis). Demonstrating the components were 'well-known and conventional' weighs against finding an inventive concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claiming a machine or tangible device is not dispositive
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if a claim is framed as an improved machine (a 'tangible system'), that fact alone does not guarantee eligibility under §101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Alice and In re TLI: courts look beyond form (e.g., 'machine') to substance — whether the claim improves technology or merely applies an abstract idea using generic machinery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive concept requirement at step two
rubrics_metrics.description: At step two, the claim must include an 'inventive concept' — meaning elements or combination that transform the abstract idea into a patent-eligible application, rather than merely invoking well-understood, routine, conventional components.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mere novelty/allowance in prosecution or the fact that conventional hardware is 'vital' to implementation does not satisfy step two (see SAP Am. v. InvestPic, Two-Way Media). The claimed features must add more than routine, conventional activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty/allowance/prosecution history are separate from eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Novelty (§102), obviousness (§103), and allowance over prior art in prosecution do not, by themselves, establish §101 eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow Diehr and SAP Am.: demonstrate that even if claim elements are novel or were allowed over references, eligibility requires analysis under Alice; novelty is not sufficient to confer eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mismatch between specification detail and claim breadth undermines eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: If the specification describes particular detailed configurations as the inventive advance but the asserted claims are drafted broadly (e.g., claiming a simpler or more generic configuration), that breadth mismatch supports a finding that the claim is directed to an abstract idea rather than the specific technical improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to test whether the claim actually captures the specific improvements disclosed; the presence of detailed embodiments in the spec does not save broadly drafted claims that cover only the abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciting a generic environment to carry out an abstract idea is an anti-pattern
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that merely provide a 'generic environment' in which to carry out an abstract idea (e.g., listing conventional components as the environment) fail to add inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re TLI example: physical components 'merely provide a generic environment in which to carry out the abstract idea' and thus do not confer eligibility. Evaluate whether the components meaningfully constrain or improve the implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conventional components 'behave as expected' supports ineligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: If the recited physical components behave exactly as expected according to their ordinary use, this supports finding no inventive concept under Alice step two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite In re TLI: look for whether claimed components do anything unconventional or whether they simply execute their routine functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courts may determine §101 eligibility at the Rule 12(b)(6) pleadings stage
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent eligibility under §101 can be resolved at the pleadings stage when the claim language and intrinsic record (and judicially noticeable facts) make the §101 issue clear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Genetic Techs., Affinity Labs: courts can consider the patent specification and other exhibits; they need not accept allegations that contradict the intrinsic record. However, careful consideration of what facts are judicially noticeable is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of long-standing or well-known practices evidences abstraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrated, long-standing practices in the relevant field (e.g., photographers using multiple pictures to enhance each other for over a century) support that the claimed idea is an abstract practice rather than a patentable technological improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When historical or field practice is undisputed or judicially noticeable, it can be considered at the pleadings stage to show the idea is conventional or abstract (Affinity Labs, district court reliance).
